data.title: Cotton claims Lutnick ignored his 'many letters' warning of chip sales to China
data.description:
Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) said Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored his warnings about U.S. AI chips being smuggled into China, long before reports surfaced about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about these Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously,” Cotton said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal published Friday.

Cotton, who recently won his reelection campaign in Arkansas and chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Journal Lutnick and his deputies ignored correspondence for over a year about companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips, including Singapore-based company Megaspeed — at the center of Huang’s high-profile departure from the company.

The GOP senator said he sent a letter to Lutnick calling for an investigation into Megaspeed in October 2025.

Alice Huang, a former executive and major shareholder at Megaspeed, was accused of illegally smuggled AI chips into China while developing a “close relationship” with the former Nvidia CEO.

The tech giant’s chief resigned on Nov. 12 as these reports garnered national attention. The resignation came a day after The New York Times reported Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.

The incident has sparked questions and calls for transparency on both sides of the aisle.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats, Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (N.Y.), are pressing Lutnick for information about the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Lutnick Thursday.

On the Republican side, Rep. Brett Guthrie (Ky.), chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, requested earlier this week that interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Lutnick appear before the panel to answer questions.

data.title: House to consider modified version of Protect College Sports Act
data.description:
The House will consider a slightly modified version of the Protect College Sports Act, a landmark bill governing college sports, as Congress aims to pass it into law before the end of the year.

The bill already passed the Senate in a sweeping bipartisan vote in late September.

After months of chaos surrounding player eligibility, the transfer portal, name, image and likeness (NIL) money and a slew of lawsuits, a bipartisan group of lawmakers have stressed the need to pass the bill as soon as possible. 

The act would give the NCAA the authority to enforce its own rules and shield it from lawsuits, one of the single biggest changes aimed at resolving a patchwork of rulings around the country that have left player eligibility uncertain and different across different jurisdictions.

The House’s latest tweak raises the cap on teams permitted in a conference from 20 to 22, opening the door to further conference realignment and expansion.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), one of the bill’s co-sponsors and biggest supporters, along with Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), stressed the need for change in a Senate floor speech advocating for the bill.

“Now I know some argue that college sports are doing just fine. They point to high television ratings, enthusiastic fan bases, and packed stadiums,” Cruz said. ”But popularity does not demonstrate that the system is healthy. It simply proves that the system is worth saving.”

The bill is backed by President Trump and GOP House leadership, but the clock is ticking on final passage — given some Democrats’ concerns about the bill, it may need to pass before the end of the year, after which Democrats will take a sizable majority in both chambers of Congress.

Trump praised the Senate’s passage of the bill back in September, calling it a “really big deal.”

“It will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Also supporting the bill is the NCAA and many of the top conferences, including the Big 10 and Southeastern conferences.

data.title: Live updates: House races uncalled nearly 3 weeks post-election; Congress recesses
data.description:
Lawmakers are leaving Capitol Hill on Saturday after a jam-packed week of moving bills and confirming appointments, with the 119th Congress seeking to see through its legislative priorities before it permanently adjourns in January.

Leaders on both sides of the aisle, including Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), expressed frustration this week with Congress members’ low attendance in the lame duck session — especially with bills on permitting reform and Iran war powers reached the floor. Johnson urged his GOP colleagues to “show up and vote” for their remaining days in office.

Meanwhile, Democrats are still waiting to see what their final tally will be in the lower chamber, especially after this week’s leadership elections. Some House races are still undecided almost three weeks after Election Day, many of which have the potential to bolster the Democratic majority. Insiders can read more from The Hill’s Julia Mueller on the outstanding contests here.

President Trump will remain in Washington, D.C., this weekend following his high-stakes trip to Asia, during which he engaged in a rare trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump held a 90-minute press briefing Friday afternoon to discuss the visit, though the conference quickly pivoted to other topics — including recent tech outages, the latest on Iran’s reported “dirty bomb” threat and how he will work with Democrats in January.

Follow live below.

data.title: License plate scanners defy the Constitution — courts must uphold drivers' privacy rights
data.description:
A federal court in northern Oklahoma has set an important example for how courts should address Fourth Amendment challenges to automatic license plate readers.

Just last month, in United States v. Kyle, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma granted a motion to suppress evidence collected via automatic license plate readers. Based on nothing more than an out-of-state plate, a Tulsa County deputy sheriff entered Melisa Kyle’s license plate number into a system database and, with a single search, obtained a month’s worth of her location history across multiple states — all without a warrant.

Kyle argued that the warrantless search of her location history violated her Fourth Amendment rights. The court agreed.

This decision marks the first time a federal court has held that the government’s warrantless collection and use of historical license plate location data violates the Constitution. Other courts confronting these increasingly pervasive surveillance systems should follow its lead.

In U.S. v. Knotts (1983), the Supreme Court ruled that a person “traveling in an automobile on public thoroughfares has no reasonable expectation of privacy in his movements.” This ruling has become a favorite precedent invoked by proponents of automatic license plate readers since, they argue, the readers capture only public movements. But that reasoning does not hold up when comparing the technologies involved in these cases. 

In Knotts, police used a primitive radio transmitter to follow a suspect’s vehicle on a single journey. The device merely supplemented the officers’ own surveillance. Today’s automatic readers are a different beast entirely. These systems routinely photograph passing vehicles, record their locations, and store that information in searchable databases. With a few keystrokes, law enforcement can piece together weeks or months of a person’s movements, without any suspicion of wrongdoing.

The distinction is not merely one of technological sophistication, but of the sheer scale, ease and intrusiveness of the surveillance.

Other major decisions in recent years have recognized the importance of considering technological advances when determining how the Fourth Amendment constrains the government in its use of surveillance technologies. 

Less than a decade ago, in Carpenter v. United States, the Supreme Court stated that “a person does not surrender all Fourth Amendment protection by venturing into the public sphere.” The court held there that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy “in the whole of their physical movements.”

In Carpenter, the court recognized that the government’s use of cell-site location information to track a person’s movements over an extended period can violate this reasonable expectation of privacy. Even when those movements occur publicly, an extensive record can reveal intimate details about a person’s life. 

In June, the Supreme Court built on Carpenter’s principles in Chatrie v. U.S., holding that the government’s acquisition of cellphone location history constitutes a Fourth Amendment search regardless of the amount of data collected. The court considered as critical factors the surveillance’s retrospective nature, its potential for indiscriminate use, its low cost and ease of deployment, and its ability to reveal sensitive information through both short- and long-term tracking. 

The Kyle ruling applied these same principles to automatic license plate readers, which similarly allow the government to systematically collect and retrospectively search location histories. Like cellphone location data, these records can reveal far more about a person’s life than any individual observation on a public road.

Perhaps most troubling is that the automatic reader system allows the collection of vast amounts of location data about ordinary Americans who are not suspected of any wrongdoing, and who often do not even realize they are being tracked in the first place. Rather than identifying a suspect and then conducting surveillance, these systems allow police to collect data indiscriminately and look for evidence of wrongdoing later. The ease and efficiency of this technology make it all the more important that courts impose meaningful constitutional limits on its use.

The Fourth Amendment was not written with automatic license plate readers in mind, but its protections were never meant to become obsolete as technology evolves. By recognizing the constitutional implications of prolonged, warrantless location tracking, Kyle offers an approach that accounts for the realities of modern surveillance. 

Other courts confronting these systems should recognize the distinction between observing a car on a public road and giving the government the ability to reconstruct a person’s movements over weeks or months. Technological advances may have transformed the government’s surveillance capabilities, but they have not diminished Americans’ Fourth Amendment rights.

Andreia Trifoi is litigation counsel at the New Civil Liberties Alliance.

data.title: California State Bar places Katie Zacharia under investigation
data.description:
The California State Bar Association is investigating former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, a newly-released letter shows, after a watchdog group filed a complaint accusing her of violating the law.

Zacharia served a brief five-day stint as press secretary, but during that period, reporting emerged that she had never passed the bar exam despite claiming to be an attorney.

Nonprofit watchdog group Campaign for Accountability (CfA) wrote a letter to the state bar on Oct. 14, saying Zacharia had broken California law, asking the bar association to open an investigation.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” CfA executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a release about the group’s letter. “The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

The state bar responded Nov. 6 in a letter recently made public, confirming it had opened an investigation.

California law prohibits anyone who is not licensed by the state bar from presenting themselves as a lawyer, and a conviction is a misdemeanor “punishable by up to one year in a county jail or by a fine of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment.”

A spokesperson for Zacharia called the allegations “baseless” and “politically motivated” in a statement to the Los Angeles Times.

Zacharia was announced as White House press secretary a few weeks after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who had served in the role since President Trump returned to office. The president promoted Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her for the role, though that was not a requirement for the role.

The complaint from the CfA specifically outlines times when she claimed to be an attorney, including several on-air appearances as a legal analyst.

“She has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 Fox News appearances since March 2025, has claimed to have served as ‘outside counsel’ to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and listed herself as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a California-based nonprofit, from January 2024 to March 2025,” the CfA said in its release about the complaint.

After completing one short press briefing, reporting emerged that she was not on record in any state for passing the bar, and Trump announced her departure after just a few days on the job.

Kuppersmith praised the state bar’s decision to launch an investigation.

“Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” she said in a Thursday release. “We’re pleased the California Bar is taking this matter seriously and investigating.”

data.title: FBI looking into possible breach of its crime database: Report
data.description:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is looking into a potential breach of its nationwide criminal information database, a second breach in recent months coming on the heels of nationwide technology outages.

The agency’s National Crime Information Center, which is used to connect federal, state and local authorities for nationwide information, was breached by apparent hackers, according to a report from CNN on Friday.

The Hill has reached out to the FBI for comment.

The attack comes as the country is recovering from widespread technology outages in the past week which impacted flights, banks, internet services and more.

On Nov. 12, Microsoft faced global outages that impacted its platforms Outlook and Teams. A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Authorities attributed FAA incident to an overload of data on routers.

Customers of several banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo had trouble accessing their accounts on Monday.

Speculations flared over whether the outages were linked to a cyberattack, but Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly said that is not the case.

Even though officials have said cybercrime was not at the center of the recent outages, the phenomenon has certainly emerged in the recent months with multiple incidents related to hacking.

In September, the FBI was targeted by the group ShinyHunters, involving sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website, according to CNN. A cybersecurity executive and ransomware expert from Canada was arrested and is facing charges related to the attack.

Earlier this month, the FBI cracked down on North Korean hackers who had stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 ​months using a social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer.”

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance faced a $6.3 billion hack in October that prompted the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. It also led other cryptocurrency firms to freeze around $3 billion in assets.

Following the recent incidents, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security announced a new hub to combat cybercrime on Wednesday.

“It gives investigators tools to triage victim complaints and map the networks responsible,” the Justice Department said in a statement.

data.title: Trump dangled a nuclear jobs boom — Now comes the fine print
data.description:
Washington has struggled for decades to find a state willing to permanently host spent fuel from nuclear power plants. Last summer, the Trump administration achieved a political breakthrough. It enticed five governors to the negotiating table with a bargain: nuclear waste would be bundled with tens of billions in investment as well as tens or hundreds of thousands of new jobs. 

That bargain looks different today. 

When the Department of Energy pitched Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses to states in January, it described mega sites that could hold everything from uranium enrichment, advanced reactors and nuclear fuel fabrication to advanced manufacturing, data centers, spent fuel recycling and waste disposal. A hypothetical campus, the department suggested, could directly employ 50,000 workers, support 100,000 to 150,000 indirect jobs and require 10,000 to 20,000 new housing units. 

In September, Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish defined success as at least three or four nuclear campuses running in 10 to 20 years. At January’s top figure, that would mean 600,000 to 800,000 jobs. At the Department of Energy’s lower figures floated in July — up to $50 billion in capital investment and nearly 25,000 jobs per campus — that is roughly 75,000 to 100,000 jobs. What governor wouldn’t want to explore numbers like these?

But nearly 10 months later, the vision has collided with reality. 

First, where would the personnel come from? The Energy Department’s own employment reports count just over 70,000 people working in the American nuclear energy sector in 2025. Sixty-five percent of nuclear power and fuel employers reported hiring challenges last year. Another survey found that only 23 percent of nuclear workers were under 30. A nuclear campus would also have to compete with advanced manufacturing and data centers for electricians and technicians.

Second, why did department officials pitch such unrealistic timelines? In January, the visoin was for initial nuclear campus facilities “online in the 2027 timeframe.” But the Sept. 30 target for host agreements has come and gone. On Nov. 10, Energy Secretary Chris Wright acknowledged that spent fuel disposal outside Nevada’s Yucca Mountain site requires legislative change. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tenn.) hoped to take action during Congress’ lame-duck session. Now, he says it may have to wait for the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress.

A week after Trump’s midterm rebuke, American Nuclear Society head Craig Piercy described a more plausible scenario. Some in the nuclear sector, he noted, worry that the near-term economic benefits of spent fuel recycling — a centerpiece of Trump’s nuclear campus plan — were oversold to states. Piercy, who supports the program, anticipated that the first projects would be limited public-private demonstrations of spent fuel transportation, recycling, storage and disposal technologies. “Even that is a ways off,” he acknowledged.

This is a welcome dose of realism. The Energy Department gambled with its own credibility earlier this year when it lent gravitas to the Trump administration’s promise-the-moon bluster. 

The department’s campus site selections are expected this year or early next. Before that happens, residents of states still at the table deserve to know how much of Trump’s original bargain their governor can secure. A handful of demonstration projects, after all, would bring in a fraction of the new jobs that Trump’s Energy Department initially invited communities, families and businesses to imagine.

A vigilant public should ask: Which facilities will actually be built? Who will pay for them? Will any really open around 2027? When will employment tick up? How many jobs will be permanent? Did state negotiators secure a strong benefits package? Can a community walk away if it feels its governor was hoodwinked? Was the Trump administration’s January pitch too good to be true?

It is unclear whether the Department of Energy’s job creation scenarios reflect an earnest ambition, careless arithmetic, a trumped-up sales pitch or an accurate accounting of the hosting agreements to follow. But if the bold economic vision that initially brought governors to the table has since fallen away — while communities are still asked to accept long-term nuclear waste commitments — then Trump’s political breakthrough may, in hindsight, look more like sleight of hand.

Vincent Ialenti is a former U.S. Department of Energy senior program manager and a senior research fellow at Tampere University in Finland. He is the author of “Longstorming: Beyond the Age of Haste.”

data.title: Former defense secretary suggests Iran war may last until 2029: 'It's just gonna take a long time'
data.description:
Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper said on Friday the ongoing war in Iran would go into 2027 but questioned whether it could go into as far as 2029, noting it “takes time.”

“Well, it’s definitely gonna go into 2027 … the question is, does it roll into 2028 and even 2029? Right, and it all depends on the strategy,” Esper said during an appearance on NewsNation, the Hill’s broadcasting partner.

Esper said he has advocated for the strategy of an “economic blockade” that President Trump is pursuing, adding, “it takes a very patient disciplined strategy that’s internationalized and that you slowly choke out the Iranians so that they eventually come to the negotiating table in a credible way.”

He emphasized that the strategy seems to be working, citing high inflation in Iran and the considerable drop in Iran’s currency, Rial.

“It’s just gonna take a long time,” Esper said.

The conflict in Iran was a major issue for voters in the days leading up to the midterm elections, where Democrats secured a sweeping victory taking control of both chambers of the Congress. In a Gallup poll released before the midterms, roughly 77 percent of voters said the war would be an “extremely” or “very” important issue when casting their vote.

Following the GOP’s midterm losses, Vance placed the blame on the war saying, “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

On Friday, during a press conference following the president’s trip to China, Vance deflected on a question of whether the war was worth the GOP’s losses, saying, “The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”

“The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we should be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism,” Vance said, adding his “job is to support the president of the United States.”

Esper said Vance “clearly” does not support the war “fully the way the president would expect.”

He agreed with Vance’s initial assessment of the midterm results, saying, “It was very clear that the two top issues for the reason why Democrats came out and many Republicans either stayed home or voted for the other side was affordability and the Iran war.”

Esper warned that “losing both the house and Senate means that the Trump agenda is largely dead at least in domestic policy.”

“There’ll be constraints placed on him from a foreign policy perspective as the Democrats type appropriations,” he added.

data.title: Democrats want 'Medicare for More.' Then comes the hard part
data.description:
Democrats are coalescing around a plan to expand Medicare coverage to more Americans when they take control of Congress in January, a consensus policy that could bridge a divide between the party’s liberal and moderate wings. 

Both sides agree that they want to pursue “Medicare for More” quickly next year. But as Democrats eye ways to quickly lower costs, internal divisions over whether to push for “Medicare for All” could complicate a longer-term agenda for healthcare reform. 

Last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whom Democrats nominated to be Speaker next term, outlined a plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, cover children under 18 years old and expand Medicare coverage for dental, vision and hearing benefits.  

Jeffries also emphasized an immediate focus on reversing Medicaid cuts under the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and restoring the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) temporary enhanced premium tax credits that expired at the end of last year.  

“Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” Jeffries said during a press conference Tuesday. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable.”  

In the past, Democrats have been split between those who support Medicare for All and those who prefer incremental changes that don’t eliminate private insurance.  

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.   

But at least for now, the factions appear united in moving toward a more middle ground.  

Lawmakers in the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) welcomed what Jeffries outlined but emphasized they believe it’s only the first step in the broader march toward single-payer healthcare.  

Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), a CPC member, said he believes Jeffries’s immediate Medicare expansion plan is “very achievable.” 

“I think we have such a large majority that this step forward is going to be something that we’re going to be able to accomplish,” he said. “But our first step is undoing a lot of the Big Beautiful Bill stuff.” 

Frost noted that the incremental Medicare expansion proposal has also received support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), the longtime standard-bearer for Medicare for All who is expected to chair the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions next Congress. 

Sanders on Wednesday praised Jeffries’s Medicare expansion plan, dubbing it “the first year [of] Medicare for All.” 

“I think the word is getting out that it is no longer, from a political point of view, from a policy point of view, good enough to tinker around the edges,” Sanders said. “Yes, we have to protect those people who lost their Medicaid, ACA premiums — I’m all in on that. But I think increasingly the American people and elected officials understand the current healthcare system is broken.” 

Shortly after the elections, Sanders outlined his own plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age by 10 years, include vision and dental care in Medicare, and guarantee health insurance for all children through age 19.  

El-Sayed also jumped in this week to back the House leader’s proposal as a “great start.”  

The Michigan Democrat made instituting a single-payer healthcare system a key tenet of his Senate campaign.  

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, advocates are looking to set the agenda with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election.  

Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), another CPC member, expressed uncertainty Thursday about the ability to get Trump’s signature on a Medicare expansion package.  

“I don’t know if we’re going to be able to do very much with Trump, but I do think that the first steps are really critical, and putting back funding to an infrastructure that has been starved is important too,” Grijalva said.  

The progressive lawmaker, who supports Medicare for All as a long-term goal, acknowledged the challenges associated with an immediate transition to a universal single-payer healthcare system.  

“Ideally, we want to get to Medicare for All relatively quickly, but I even heard Sen. Sanders say if we just flip a switch, you know, we could collapse a system that is already struggling,” she said. “So we don’t want to do that.” 

If the Medicare expansion idea gains traction in the next Congress, progressives will want to see real movement toward Medicare for All, something neither Jeffries nor Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has endorsed. That would likely create internal tensions within the party as it looks ahead to the 2028 presidential election. 

But at the same time, letting a bill come to the floor during the Trump presidency would catapult Medicare for All directly into the 2028 conversation and show Democrats no longer fear attacks about taking away people’s private insurance.  

Rep. Ami Bera (D-Calif.), a physician and member of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, said a workable long-term plan will be contingent on factors like cost and coverage.  

Bera stressed a more immediate focus on reversing cuts made under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as H.R. 1.  

“Those aren’t the long-term solutions, but those at least give us time to lower costs for Americans, increase access, and then I think we can work on the longer-term ideas,” he said.  

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a “single government plan.”    

A national debate would likely include more details about costs and trade-offs that aren’t being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.  

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) praised Jeffries’s plan as a “very meaningful and substantive proposal” that could bridge divides within the Democratic Party over long-term healthcare goals.  

“It would undoubtedly win the support of a lot of people who want to move towards a national health system with Medicare for All, and I think it could gain a lot of support from other people who understand the huge gaps that exist,” Raskin said. “So I think that’s a shrewd proposal for him to advance.” 

Nathaniel Weixel contributed.

data.title: Virginia reports first measles-related death of 2026
data.description:
A young child in Virginia died after testing positive for measles, the state’s health department said Friday, marking the first death tied to the illness in the state this year.

The department said the child was aged 0-4 but declined to share further identifying information, such as vaccination status or other details related to the death, due to privacy concerns.

The fatal case in Virginia is the second reported measles-associated death since the Pan-American Health Organization announced this week it revoked the U.S.’s measles elimination status, declaring the disease endemic amid an ongoing outbreak.

In 2026, states have reported a total of 12 deaths tied to the disease, though the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) currently count currently sits at six as of Friday night.

The discrepancies between these reported death tolls have become a source of contention between state officials and federal ones, specifically Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — who has sent mixed signals on the administration’s vaccine stance in recent months.

Virginia has recorded 220 measles cases so far this year, with just 1 percent in unvaccinated individuals, according to the commonwealth’s dashboard. More cases are concentrated in Charlotte County, a rural county in Southside Virginia, than anywhere else in the state.

Only a few patients have been hospitalized statewide, and the University of Virginia medical center revealed Monday it was treating a patient with measles — warning students to isolate if they develop symptoms and check their vaccination status.

But no state has been hit harder with the measles outbreak than Pennsylvania, which accounts for more than 25 percent of cases in the entire country and a majority of states’ reported deaths.

The CDC continues to say the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the most effective way to fight the infection, but just a few months ago, Trump signed an executive order recommending breaking up the MMR vaccine into three doses. The shot is typically given once at 12-15 months and again at 4-6 years.

At an event in the Oval Office in August, Trump suggested the combined shot was “lethal” without providing any evidence.
